Judgment :

The present criminal appeal is preferred by the State against the Judgment and Order dated 21/07/2004 passed by the learned Chief Judicial Magistrate, Raigad at Alibag,
in Regular Criminal Case No. 38 of 1997,

entities.text: Chief Judicial Magistrate, Raigad at Alibag
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
whereby the respondents (original accused)
came to be acquitted of the offences punishable under Section 7(1) read with Sections 2(ia)(a), 2(ia)(c) and 2(ia)(j), read with Rules 23 and 28 and Sections 16 and 17 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (for short, "the PFA Act").

2. The prosecution case, in brief, is that on 23 August 1996 at about 1:30 p.m., the Food Inspector visited the premises of M/s. Hotel Sea View at Alibag and purchased 600 grams of chilli powder from accused No.1 for analysis.
The sample was divided into three parts, sealed and forwarded in accordance with the procedure contemplated under the PFA Act and Rules.

The Public Analyst reported that the sample contained red and orange oil-soluble synthetic colour and did not conform t o t h e p r e s c r i b e d s t a n d a r d s . A f t e r o b t a i n i n g r e q u i s i t e c o n s e n t , p r o s e c u t i o n ____________________________________________ 24 February 2026 Chitra Sonawane 1-A-1316-2004.doc was launched.
3.

The learned trial Court, upon appreciation of evidence of P.W.1 (Food Inspector), P.W.2 (Clerk from Local Health Authority) and P.W.3 (Panch witness), acquitted the accused by holding that the prosecution failed to establish strict compliance with mandatory procedural requirements and failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
4. It is a settled principle of criminal jurisprudence that an order of acquittal strengthens the presumption of innocence.
The appellate court will not interfere unless the conclusions drawn by The State Of Maharashtra vs Samir Kamlakar Patil And Ors.

the trial court are perverse, manifestly illegal, or wholly unsupported by evidence.
If two views are possible, the one favourable to the accused must be adopted.
5. The learned Magistrate noticed a material inconsistency in the prosecution case.

In the complaint,
it is stated that the chilli powder was divided into three parts and kept in clean, dry polythene bags.
However, during evidence, P.W.1 deposed that each part was kept in bottles.
The panchanama also refers to bottles.
The Food Inspector failed to satisfactorily explain this inconsistency.

The nature ____________________________________________ 24 February 2026 Chitra Sonawane 1-A-1316-2004.doc of container used for preserving the sample is not a trivial detail but goes to the root of compliance with Rule 14 of the PFA Rules, which mandates that samples must be taken in clean and suitable containers so as to prevent contamination.
The trial Court rightly observed that the prosecution failed to establish with certainty whether the sample was kept in bottles or polythene bags.
Such inconsistency creates a serious doubt regarding the integrity of the sampling process.
6. Evidence of P.W.2 reveals that he could not firmly state whether notices under Section 13(2) of the PFA Act were duly served upon all accused.
The postal acknowledgements bore similar signatures and there was no cogent evidence to prove effective service.

The right under Section 13(2)
to have the sample analyzed by the Central Food Laboratory is a valuable statutory safeguard.
Any ambiguity regarding compliance must operate in favour of the accused.
7. Furthermore, the panch witness did not fully support the prosecution case.
The trial Court carefully scrutinized the evidence and found material discrepancies in the testimony of P.W.1.
In p r o s e c u t i o n s u n d e r t h e P F A A c t , s t r i c t _
compliance with statutory safeguards is mandatory.
The burden lies squarely upon the prosecution to establish that every procedural requirement has been adhered to.
The learned Magistrate, after analyzing the oral and documentary evidence, arrived at a plausible view that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
Upon independent reappreciation of the entire evidence on record, this Court finds that the view taken by the Trial Court is a possible and reasonable view based on evidence.
The findings recorded by the learned Magistrate cannot be said to be perverse, illegal, or contrary to the material on record so as to warrant interference in an appeal against acquittal.
8. In criminal jurisprudence, benefit of doubt must necessarily go to the accused.
The prosecution having failed to remove reasonable doubt regarding compliance with mandatory provisions, the acquittal deserves to be confirmed.
Accordingly the present Criminal Appeal stands dismissed.
The Judgment and Order dated 21/07/2004 passed by the Learned Chief Judicial Magistrate, Raigad at Alibag in Regular Criminal Case No. 38 of 1997 is hereby confirmed.
